questions.question: What is the most important first question when reviewing a patient’s anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy?
choices: Why is the medication prescribed, and what exact agent, dose, and timing are being used?
Does the patient call it a blood thinner?
Is the medication a tablet?
Has the patient taken it for more than one month?
questions.explanation: The indication and exact medication determine the risks of interruption, monitoring needs, interactions, and safe next steps.

questions.question: Why should an FNP avoid blanket advice to hold anticoagulation for a few days?
choices: Interruption risk depends on indication, agent, thrombotic risk, procedure, renal function, and the responsible prescriber’s plan
All anticoagulants are identical
Holding a medication never changes thrombotic risk
Every procedure has the same bleeding risk
questions.explanation: Stopping antithrombotic therapy can be dangerous in some indications. Peri-procedural and interruption decisions must be individualized.

questions.question: Which group of information is essential in an anticoagulation safety interview?
choices: Exact agent, indication, last dose, missed/extra doses, new medicines, trauma, procedures, and bleeding/thrombotic symptoms
Only the patient’s age
Only the INR value
Only the name of the pharmacy
questions.explanation: Safe assessment needs both medication facts and clinical context. Bleeding and thrombosis can be subtle or urgent.

questions.question: Why can renal or hepatic dysfunction increase anticoagulation risk?
choices: It can change drug exposure and bleeding risk, especially during acute illness or dehydration
It has no relationship to medication safety
It permanently eliminates thrombotic risk
It means every drug should be stopped immediately
questions.explanation: Kidney and liver function affect anticoagulant safety. Evaluate trends, acute illness, interactions, and the patient’s specific regimen.

questions.question: A patient on an anticoagulant reports black stools, dizziness, and weakness. What is the best FNP priority?
choices: Assess for significant bleeding and hemodynamic instability and arrange urgent or emergency evaluation
Schedule a routine follow-up next month
Tell the patient to take an extra dose
Assume the stool color is harmless without assessment
questions.explanation: Black stools with systemic symptoms can signal gastrointestinal bleeding and require prompt assessment and emergency escalation when concerning.

questions.question: Which statement best describes direct oral anticoagulants?
choices: They do not use routine INR monitoring like warfarin but still require review of adherence, organ function, interactions, indication, and procedures
They are set-and-forget medications
They never interact with other drugs
They are appropriate for every thrombotic indication
questions.explanation: DOACs reduce some monitoring burdens but still have important safety limitations and require ongoing individualized review.

questions.question: A patient taking an anticoagulant has a fall with head strike and mild headache. What is the safest action?
choices: Arrange urgent evaluation according to emergency guidance rather than giving phone-based skip-dose advice
Assume it is safe because the headache is mild
Double the next dose after the fall
Wait until the next routine appointment
questions.explanation: Head trauma in an anticoagulated patient can involve occult bleeding. It requires clinical assessment rather than casual medication adjustment.

questions.question: Why should over-the-counter NSAIDs, supplements, and antiplatelet medications be reviewed in patients on anticoagulation?
choices: They can add bleeding risk or create clinically important interactions
They are never relevant to prescription medications
They prevent all thrombotic events
They replace the need for renal monitoring
questions.explanation: Medication reconciliation must include nonprescription products because they may affect hemostasis, drug exposure, kidney function, or bleeding risk.

questions.question: A patient with atrial fibrillation develops sudden facial droop and speech difficulty despite reporting medication adherence. What should the FNP do?
choices: Activate EMS for a time-critical stroke evaluation
Debate medication adherence before acting
Tell the patient to drive to the clinic
Recommend an extra anticoagulant dose at home
questions.explanation: Antithrombotic therapy lowers but does not eliminate stroke risk. New focal neurologic symptoms require emergency evaluation.

questions.question: What is the safest general approach to anticoagulant reversal or peri-procedural planning?
choices: Follow current medication-specific emergency or procedural protocols with the responsible care team
Use the same instruction for every anticoagulant
Base it only on whether a procedure sounds minor
Ask the patient to choose the stop and restart dates
questions.explanation: Reversal, interruption, bridging, and restart decisions are high risk and depend on the drug, indication, timing, organ function, procedure, and current clinical state.
